title: Bending 'cathode rays' revealed the electron, about 1,800 times lighter than any atom

cover.alt: A glass deflection tube inside a large coil, with a glowing blue beam of electrons curving upwards across a gridded screen.

body: Put a high voltage across two electrodes in a glass tube pumped almost empty, and something streams from the negative electrode, the cathode. In 1876 Eugen Goldstein named it **cathode rays**. The rays are invisible, but they make glass, phosphor screens or leftover gas glow, and magnets bend them. In 1897 J. J. Thomson measured them and showed they were particles around 1,800 times lighter than hydrogen, the lightest atom: the first subatomic particle ever found, later named the electron.

slides.alt: Inside a glass tube set in a large coil, a glowing blue beam of electrons curves upwards; as the coil's current is turned down, the curve flattens until the beam runs straight.
slides.caption: In the coil's magnetic field, the beam of electrons curves upwards. As the current in the coil is turned down, the beam straightens out.

slides.heading: An electron next to the lightest atom
slides.note: Thomson's 1897 result: around 1,800 times lighter than hydrogen

events.text: Plücker and Hittorf first see the rays

slides.heading: Why a magnet bends the beam
slides.text: A moving charge in a magnetic field feels a sideways push, now called the Lorentz force. William Crookes put a magnet across the neck of his tube and saw the beam bend at right angles to the field, just as a current-carrying wire is pushed in an electric motor.

slides.question: What did Thomson originally call the particles in cathode rays?
slides.explanation: He called them corpuscles. The name electron came from George Johnstone Stoney, who had proposed such particles in 1874.
